en: The Sūtra of the Ascertainment of Meaning.
Homage to the glorious Mañjughoṣa.
The Blessed One said: "And what, monks, is this Dharma discourse called the *Arthaviniścaya*? It is that which was spoken: the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging."
The eighteen elements,
the twelve sense bases,
and the twelve-linked dependent origination.
The four noble truths;
the twenty-two faculties;
the four meditative absorptions.
The four formless attainments;
the four divine abidings;
the four analytical knowledges.
The four cultivations of concentration;
the four foundations of mindfulness;
the four right efforts.
The four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties,
and the five powers.
The seven factors of enlightenment;
the noble eightfold path;
and the sixteen aspects of mindfulness of breathing.
The four factors of stream-entry;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
the thirty-two marks of a great man,
and the eighty minor marks.
Monks, this is the summary of the Dharma discourse entitled "The Determination of Meaning."
(1) In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates?
They are as follows: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, [the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness].
The aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
Monks, these are the five aggregates.
(2) In this regard, monks, what are the five aggregates of clinging?

They are as follows: the aggregate of clinging to form; the aggregate of clinging to feeling; [the aggregate of clinging to perception; the aggregate of clinging to mental formations; and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness].
The aggregate of clinging to perception; the aggregate of clinging to mental formations; the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
Monks, these are the five aggregates of clinging.
(3) In this regard, monks, what are the eighteen elements? They are as follows: the eye element and the form element.
The element of eye-consciousness;
the element of the ear; the element of sound.
The auditory consciousness element;
the olfactory element; the odor element.
The element of olfactory consciousness,
the element of the tongue, and the element of taste.
The tongue-consciousness element,
the body element,
and the contact element.
The element of body-consciousness,
the mind-element, and the mental-object-element.
The mind-consciousness element.
Monks, these are called the eighteen elements.
(4) In this regard, monks, what are the twelve bases (*āyatana*)? Namely: the internal base of the eye and the internal base of visible forms.
The ear is the internal sense base;
sound is the external sense base;
the nose is the internal sense base.
Odor is the external sense base;
the tongue is the internal sense base;
taste is the external sense base.
The body is the internal sense base;
contact is the external sense base;
the mind is the internal sense base.
Dharma is the external sense base.
These, monks, are called the twelve sense bases.
(5) In this regard, monks, what is dependent origination with its twelve factors?
With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness.
Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form;
conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact.
Conditioned by contact is feeling;
conditioned by feeling is craving;
conditioned by craving is grasping.
With clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise.
Thus there comes to be the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
From the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.
From the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming.
From the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
(a) In that regard, what is ignorance?
It is that which is non-knowing regarding the past limit and non-knowing regarding the future limit.
Ignorance regarding the past and the future; ignorance regarding the internal;
ignorance regarding the external.
Ignorance regarding the internal and external; ignorance regarding karma; ignorance regarding its maturation.
Ignorance regarding the ripening of karma; ignorance regarding what is well-done;
ignorance regarding what is ill-done.
Ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;
ignorance regarding the cause;
ignorance regarding the fruit.
Ignorance regarding cause and effect;
ignorance regarding phenomena produced from causes;
and ignorance regarding dependent origination.
Ignorance regarding dependently originated phenomena;
ignorance regarding the Buddha; ignorance regarding the Dharma.
Ignorance regarding the Saṅgha; ignorance regarding suffering; ignorance regarding the origin [of suffering].
Ignorance regarding cessation;
ignorance regarding the path; ignorance regarding the wholesome.
Ignorance regarding the unwholesome;
ignorance regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena;
and ignorance regarding that which is blameworthy.
Ignorance regarding the blameless;
ignorance regarding dharmas that are blameworthy or blameless;
and ignorance regarding what is to be cultivated.
Ignorance regarding what is not to be cultivated; ignorance regarding those dharmas that are to be cultivated and those that are not to be cultivated;
and ignorance regarding that which is associated with outflows (sāsrava).
Ignorance regarding the untainted;
ignorance regarding both tainted and untainted phenomena;
and ignorance regarding the conditioned.
Ignorance regarding the unconditioned;
ignorance regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
Ignorance regarding the past;
ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding the present.
Ignorance regarding phenomena of the past, future, and present; or,
with respect to the six bases of contact, ignorance as it truly is— lack of vision, lack of clear realization, darkness, delusion, the obscurity of nescience— this is called "ignorance" (avidyā).
(ā) "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces.
What are the formative forces?
There are three types of formative forces: the bodily formative force, the vocal formative force, and the mental formative force.
In that regard, what is bodily formation? It is inhalation and exhalation,
for this is a physical phenomenon.
It is dependent on the body and bound to the body;
it exists in reliance upon the body.
Therefore, inhalation and exhalation are called "bodily formations" (kāyasaṃskāra).
What is the formative factor of speech?
Having applied thought and sustained thought, one utters speech;
not without having applied thought, nor without having sustained thought.
Therefore, applied thought and sustained thought are called the formative forces of speech.
What is the mental formation? It is the volition of one who is impassioned,
and that of the mind.
Therefore, whatever volition he has is a mental factor (caitasika),
for it is dependent upon the mind and bound to the mind.
It proceeds depending upon the mind;
therefore, volition is called a mental formation.
(i) "Consciousness has formations as its condition.
What is consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness.
Which six? Namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and nose-consciousness.
Tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
These are the six groups of consciousness.
(ī) "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises].
In this context, "name-and-form" refers to name, which consists of the four formless aggregates.
Which four?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
The aggregate of consciousness. This is "name.
What is form?
Whatever is form,
that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements.
Namely: the earth element,
the water element,
and the fire element.
The wind element.
What is the earth element? That which is heaviness and hardness.
What is the water element?
What is fluidity and what is the state of flowing?
What is the fire element (*tejodhātu*)?
It is that which is heat and that which is the state of ripening.
What is the wind element? It is that which is contraction, expansion, and lightness-and-motion;
this is the aforementioned form.
These two, being condensed together into one, are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
(u) "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
What are the six sense bases? The eye base, and so forth.
The sense base of the ear, the sense base of the nose, and the sense base of the tongue.
The sense-base of the body and the sense-base of the mind;
this is called the six sense-bases.
(ū) "With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact.
What is contact?
It consists of the six groups of contact: eye-contact, [ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact].
Ear-contact, nose-contact, and tongue-contact.
Body-contact; mind-contact.
(This is called contact.)
(e) Feeling has contact as its condition.
What is feeling?
It consists of the six types of feeling.
Which six?
Feeling born of eye-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of ear-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Feeling born of olfactory contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of gustatory contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
feeling born of tactile contact is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Feeling born of mental contact is pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
this is called feeling.
(o) Craving has feeling as its condition.
What is craving?
It consists of the six classes of craving.
Which six? Craving for forms, craving for sounds, and craving for odors.
Craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
This is called craving.
(ka) Clinging has craving as its condition.
What is clinging?
There are four kinds of clinging.
Which four? Clinging to craving and clinging to rules and observances.
The appropriation of self-feeling;
this is called appropriation.
(kha) "Existence has grasping as its condition.
What is existence?
There are three types of existence.
Which three? Existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and [existence in the realm of formlessness].
and the formless existence (ārūpyabhava).
Among these, what is sensual existence (kāmabhava)?
It is as follows: the hells (naraka).
Animals, hungry ghosts,
asuras,
and the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
They are as follows—the eight great hells.
Which are the eight? They are as follows—the hot great hells.
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, and Saṃghāta.
And there are two Rauravas:
Tapana and Pratāpana.
And Avīci.
Thus it is said.
The great hells.
Namely: Arbuda,
Nirarbuda,
and Aṭaṭa.
Hahava, huhuva, and utpala.
Padma; Mahāpadma.
Which are the six classes of gods? The gods of the Four Great Kings; the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods.
The gods who wield power over the creations of others.
In that regard, what is existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*)? It is as follows: the gods of Brahmā’s retinue (*brahmakāyika*) and the ministers of Brahmā (*brahmapurohita*).
The Mahābrahmās, the Parīttābhas, and the Apramāṇābhas.
The Ābhāsvara deities, the Parīttaśubha deities, and the Apramāṇaśubha deities.
The Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, and the Puṇyaprasavas.
The Abṛha gods; the Atapa gods; the Abṛha gods; the Sudarśana gods.
And the Akaniṣṭhas.
What are the formless realms? They are as follows: the sphere of infinite space; (AvSū, Vaidya 314) [and so forth].
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For the formless gods and those who meditate on mind-only, there are four modes of rebirth;
this is called "existence conditioned by grasping."
(ga) "Birth has existence as its condition.
What is birth? It is the birth of those various sentient beings within their respective classes of beings.
Birth, descent, and manifestation.
The manifestation of the aggregates, the acquisition of the sense bases, and the arising of the life-faculty.
This is called birth.
(g) (With birth as condition, there is aging and death. What is aging?
It is that which, within that commonality of group, consists of baldness, graying of hair, abundance of wrinkles, decrepitude, stooping, and hunchbacking.

The crookedness of the joints and the rafters; labored inhalation and exhalation with a wheezing sound (*khurukhuru*); the body being marred by spots and moles; the torso leaning forward; the need for support by a staff; the ripening and disintegration of the sense faculties; the state of being worn out and decrepit;
and the resulting sluggishness, dullness, loss, and decline.
This is called old age.
In that regard, what is death?

It is the falling away of those beings from that physical body; it is their passing away, dissolution, disappearance, death, the completion of their time, the loss of lifespan, the loss of heat, the cessation of the life-faculty, and the casting off of the aggregates.
This is called death.
This death and the aforementioned aging—
these two, when condensed together into one, are called "aging-and-death."
This, monks, is the analysis of this twelvefold dependent origination.

(6) In that regard, what are the four noble truths? They are as follows: the noble truth of suffering; the noble truth of the origin of suffering; [the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering].
The noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of suffering? It is as follows: birth is suffering;
aging is suffering.
Sickness is suffering;
death is suffering;
separation from the beloved is suffering.
Association with the unpleasant is suffering;
form is suffering;
feeling is suffering.
Perception is suffering; mental formations are suffering; consciousness is suffering.
Furthermore, that which is sought after in this manner and yet not found is also suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is as follows: this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; this is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, exhaustion, destruction, fading away, cessation, pacification, and disappearance of this very craving— which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is the noble eightfold path, beginning with right view and so forth.

For example: suppose a certain man, overcome by fever, approaches a physician who is accomplished in medical skill, has witnessed its practice, and is learned in the treatises, and says to him: "I am not at peace due to this fever; I desire that you prescribe a medicine for its pacification.
That physician would first inquire about the cause: "What have you eaten and what have you drunk?"

The patient would say to him, "I have indeed eaten curd and cucumber, and I have drunk food, drink, and buttermilk. That physician, having instructed him on the specific [nature of the ailment], would prescribe the medicine.

In the very same way, virtuous persons tormented by the great fever of birth and so forth, having approached the Tathāgata—the Great Physician of the mind, the Lord endowed with great compassion—should inquire about the Dharma that removes the fever of suffering.

To them, the Blessed One, having explained the cause known as origination (*samudaya*), would teach the Noble Eightfold Path as the great medicine and Nirvana as the bringer of peace. [Thus ends the section on] one afflicted by the defilements (*kleśa*).
By cultivating this path, one will before long attain the destruction of all suffering, go to the city of Nirvana, and achieve complete peace.
These, indeed, monks, are the four noble truths.
(7) In that regard, monks, what is the noble eightfold path?
It is as follows: right view and right intention.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this regard, monks, what is right view?
There is this world; there is the next world.
There is a father;
there is what is given; there is what is offered.
"There is the ripening of the fruits of actions that are desired or undesired, well-done or ill-done;
there are in the world those who have gone rightly and who have practiced rightly"— this,
monks, is right view.
What is right resolve? It is giving dedicated toward [the attainment of] Buddhahood and so forth, and ethical discipline dedicated toward [the attainment of] a universal monarch and so forth.
This, monks, is right intention.
What is right speech? Here, monks, it is speech that avoids harshness, falsehood, slander, and frivolous chatter; it is truthful speech.
This is called right speech.
What is right action (*samyakkarmānta*)?
It is the engagement of body, speech, and mind in the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
Among these, bodily [action] is threefold: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Vocal [action] is fourfold:
abstaining from false speech, harsh speech, slanderous speech, and frivolous chatter. Mental [action] is threefold: abstaining from covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
In that regard, what is the taking of life? It is when there is a living being,
and one perceives it as a living being.
And when one gives rise to a murderous intent and deprives [a being] of life,
this, monks, is called the taking of life.
Except in cases of negligence or through lack of perception, there is no taking of life.
In that regard, what is taking what is not given?
Taking possession of another's property with a thieving mind is taking what is not given;
except for the case of taking a small amount of the property of one's mother, father, brothers, kinsmen, or friends, which does not cause them distress—that too is taking what is not given.
In that regard, what is sexual misconduct?
It is the enjoyment of the wives of others— those protected by a husband, a king, parents, or [other guardians].
Alternatively, physical misconduct consists of acting improperly regarding place, object, or time;
thus it is threefold.
What is falsehood?
When questioned as a witness, to speak contrary to the facts or untruthfully; or to say "I am an Arhat" when one is not, as a matter for derision—this is called falsehood.
What is divisive speech? Divisive speech is speech that causes division, whether by means of what is untrue or what is true.

What is harsh speech (*pārūṣya*)? It is the act of making someone hear abusive words with the intention: "May he experience the suffering of hearing unpleasant speech," desiring to cause pain to another.
That is harsh speech.
What is frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*)?
It consists of talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of gambling, talk of intoxicants, talk of women, and talk of tales.
This is called frivolous chatter.
And that which is vocal is of four kinds.
What is covetousness (*abhidhyā*)?
It is the desire to appropriate the property of another, thinking, "May these possessions of another belong to me"; this is called covetousness.
What is ill-will (*vyāpāda*)? It is the thought of depriving another of life, or of cutting, torturing, and so forth. This is called ill-will.
What is wrong view?
It is as stated previously: "There is no this world, there is no other world," and so forth.
This threefold mental [action] is called wrong view.
Now, what is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*)?

For a monk, right livelihood consists in the absence of hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), flattery (*lapanā*), hinting (*naimittikatva*), coercion (*naiṣpeṣikatva*), and the seeking of gain through gain (*lābhena lābhapratikāṅkṣā*).
[Thus, it is] the absence of hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth.

In that regard, what is hypocrisy (*kuhanā*)? When a monk, seeing a donor, sits cross-legged on the road or in an empty house as if meditating, thinking, "I shall obtain gain and honor by being perceived as an Arhat"—
this and similar acts are called hypocrisy.
In that regard, what is flattery (*lapanā*)? Here, a monk, for the sake of gain and honor alone, says: "You are my mother;
you are my daughter."
In this way, he utters other pleasing words as well;
such speech is called "flattery."

In that regard, what is "hinting" (*naimittikatva*)? It is when a monk, having consumed his alms-food, says either once or repeatedly: "Such as this alms-food is, such is not found in the homes of other lay devotees."
However, there is no fault at all for one who speaks with a mind free from desire for gain or honor;
this is called "hinting" (naimittikatva).
In that regard, what is "importunity"? It is when a monk, having failed to receive almsfood at a certain house,
desires to have it given to him.
In that regard, he says: "Those who are not masters of giving go to hell;
you too are not masters of giving, so you clearly belong among those going to hell.
Thus, out of fear of hell, he offers alms-food to them.
And having obtained that, one enjoys it;
this is called "the state of being a gainer" (naiṣpaṣikatva).
In that regard, what is the expectation of gain for the sake of gain?
A monk first uses his own wealth to purchase fine robes and shows them to lay followers, saying, "We receive such garments from our patrons.
They, being thus enticed, then offer him those very robes.
He consumes them;
this, monks, is called a monk’s longing for gain through gain. This, monks, is wrong livelihood.
Therefore, abstention from such [wrong livelihood] is right livelihood.
In this regard, monks, what is the wrong livelihood of a lay follower? It is the sale of poison and the sale of weapons.
The selling of living beings,
the selling of intoxicants,
and the selling of meat.
The pressing of sesame and mustard seeds without having first entered [the workshop]:
this is the wrong livelihood of a lay follower; abstaining from this is the precept.
This, monks, is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?
It is frequent salutation, rising to meet [others], joining the palms in reverence, and performing acts of proper courtesy. This, monks, is called right effort.
What is right mindfulness?

Here, monks, when a monk sees a woman and lust arises, he becomes one who sees things as they truly are by way of the unattractive nature of both the external and internal bodies: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, dirt, filth, skin, and flesh."
It is full of bones, sinews, veins, kidneys, heart, liver, spleen, stomach,

intestines, mesentery, mesenteric fat, gallbladder, bile, phlegm, tears, sweat, saliva, nasal mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, brain matter, and excrement; it is filled with various kinds of impurities.
This, monks, is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
It is the four dhyānas.

Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
He dwells;

with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.
Through detachment from rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
And he experiences pleasure with the body— of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous"— and thus enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Monks, these indeed are the four dhyānas;
this is called right concentration.
This, monks, is called the noble eightfold path.
(8) What are the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*)? Namely:

the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of suffering, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of mental joy, and the faculty of mental grief.
the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of knowledge, the life-faculty,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and the faculty of knowing.
The faculty of one who has already known.
These, monks, are the twenty-two faculties.

(9) In this regard, monks, what are the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first meditative absorption, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and happiness.
Through detachment from rapture, he dwells in equanimity,
mindful and clearly comprehending.
He experiences pleasure with the body— of which the Noble Ones say, "he dwells in equanimity, mindful, and at ease"— and having attained the third dhyāna, he dwells therein.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Monks, these are the four meditative absorptions.
(10) In this regard, what are the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*)?

Here, monks, a monk dwells having suffused one quarter with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from affliction, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated; having liberated [his mind] as if it were a single mass, he dwells having attained and pervaded [it].
Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and in every direction, he dwells having pervaded this entire world in all its aspects with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— a mind free from enmity, free from ill will,
free from affliction, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, and well-cultivated— having resolved upon one quarter and attained it.

In the same way, with a mind accompanied by compassion, accompanied by sympathetic joy, and accompanied by equanimity— a mind that is free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from affliction, vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated— one resolves upon and pervades one direction.
Having attained these, he dwells therein; these are the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
(11) In this regard, what are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
There is the difficult path with sluggish superknowledge; there is the difficult path with swift superknowledge.
There is the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge;
there is the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
In that regard, what is the painful practice with slow direct knowledge?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful,
and intensely deluded.
He constantly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of intense passion; he constantly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of hatred due to his intense hatred;
he constantly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of delusion due to his intense delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties are sluggish, weak, and not swift-moving.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five supramundane faculties are weak and do not proceed swiftly, one touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) only slowly—that is, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*). This is the difficult practice with slow superknowledge (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*). In that regard, what is the difficult practice with quick superknowledge (*duḥkhā pratipat kṣiprābhijñā*)?
In this case, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate, intensely hateful,
and intensely deluded.
Because of his frequent and intense passion, he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
because of his frequent and intense hatred, he repeatedly experiences the suffering and mental distress born of hatred; [and] because of his frequent... (AvSū, Vaidya 318)
Due to the intensity of his delusion, he experiences the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties become superior, sharp, and swift-acting.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

Because these five supramundane faculties are predominant and proceed swiftly, he very quickly touches the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) concentration, that is, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the painful practice with swift direct knowledge.
In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge?
Here, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion and little hatred.
Because he has little passion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
because he has little hatred, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of hatred.
Due to having little delusion, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of delusion.
For him, these five supramundane faculties are sluggish, weak, not sharp, and not swift-moving.
Which five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because these five faculties are sluggish, dull, and do not proceed rapidly, one touches only a sluggish immediate concentration—that is, for the sake of the destruction of the outflows.
This is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge.
In that regard, what is the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge?
Here, a certain person is by nature one who has little passion, little hatred, and little delusion.
Because his passion is slight, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of passion;
because his hatred is slight, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of hatred;
because his delusion is slight, he does not frequently experience the suffering and mental distress born of delusion. For him, these...
The five supramundane faculties are superior, sharp, and swift-moving.
What are the five?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because these five faculties are superior, sharp, and swift-moving, he very quickly touches the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), namely, for the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
This is called the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
These, monks, are the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
[12] In that regard, what are the four cultivations of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*)?
... There is, monks, a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*).
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of wisdom (*prajñā*).

In this regard, what is the cultivation of concentration that, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this very body— upward from the soles of the feet and downward from the hair of the head, bounded by the skin— exactly as it is situated, exactly as it is disposed, full of various kinds of impurity, with right wisdom according to reality.

That is to say: this body is a collection of atoms that has arisen in succession and is subject to unprecedented destruction; it is porous, subject to rising and falling, and it exudes from its pores, wounds, and apertures; like an anthill, it is an abode for venomous serpents, born of those very serpents and their actions.
Ignorance is an enemy who betrays even those who have not done him wrong; it is like a bad friend who deceives;
it is as naturally fragile as a mass of foam.
Like a water bubble, it arises, breaks, and dissolves; like a mirage, it is deceptive;
like a plantain tree, it is pithless when dissected.
Like an illusion, its nature is deceptive; like a king, it disregards commands; like an enemy, it watches for an opportunity to strike.
He is untrustworthy like a thief;
he seeks one's harm like an enemy;
and he creates an obstacle to wisdom and life like an executioner.
Like an empty village, it is devoid of Māra;
like a potter's vessel, it has no limit;
and it is filled with various impurities.
It drips with impurities like a vessel of fat;
it is motionless and cruel like a snake;
it has a sharp stench like a corpse.
Like a chamber of excrement, it is a source of impurity;
like a wound, it is intolerant of being touched;
like a thorn, its purpose is to pierce.
He is difficult to serve like a wicked master;
he must be maintained through constant repair like a dilapidated house;
he must be kept afloat through constant maintenance like a worn-out boat.
It is to be guarded like an unbaked clay pot;
it is to be constantly protected like a wicked friend;
it is as unstable as a tree on a riverbank.
Like the current of a great river, it terminates in the ocean of death; like a transient, hollow shelter, it is the abode of all suffering;
and like an orphanage, it is without a protector.
It is to be won over by bribes like a thief’s door;
it is constantly beset like a frontier city;
and it is prone to collapse like a city of sand.
Like fire, he is insatiable;
like the ocean, he is difficult to fill;
like a basket for all things, he is to be avoided by those who seek to gather [merit].
It must be constantly nurtured like a young child; it must be constantly guarded against mishaps like a broken vessel;
and it is perpetually beset by afflictions like a wicked deity.
He is to be avoided like a vessel containing poison;
he is to be used for a momentary purpose like a borrowed utensil;
he is to be employed for carrying a load like a cart.
It must be understood solely by one whose mind is fixed on the Dharma.

Furthermore, monks, a monk should examine this body according to its primary and secondary causes. Here, the primary cause of the body is its origination from the semen and blood of the mother and father; the secondary causes consist of the intake of food and so forth.
Food taken in mouthfuls, as soon as it is swallowed, goes to the receptacle of phlegm (*śleṣmāśaya*).
Having reached the receptacle of phlegm, it is liquefied by the phlegm and becomes utterly impure. From the phlegm, it goes to the receptacle of bile (*pittāśaya*).
Having reached the seat of bile (*pittāśaya*), it is digested and becomes hot, then proceeds to the seat of wind (*vāyvāśaya*).
Having been cooked, once it has reached the seat of wind, it is separated by the wind into waste matter (*mala*) and into essence (*sāra*) respectively.
From the refuse come impurities such as urine and excrement;
from the essence, blood is produced,
and from blood, flesh.
From flesh comes fat; from fat, bones; from bones, marrow; from marrow...

Semen. Thus, seeing that the body is impure due to such primary and subsequent causes, a monk [should reflect]: "This body is erected upon six hundred and ten bones, joined together like a house of wretched wood by three hundred ligatures, and bound by four hundred networks of veins."
It is smeared with five hundred pieces of flesh, a mass bound together by hundreds of veins,
and bent by seven hundred veins.
It is bound together by nine hundred sinews, perforated by arteries like lattice windows,
and its vessels are shattered like a broken pot by one hundred and seven vital points (*marmans*); it is covered with eighty million hairs like blades of grass.
With the openings of the five sense-faculties and seven receptacles (or seven latent tendencies) filled with impurity.
With a handful of brain matter, with a handful of fat, and with three handfuls of muscle fat.
Six handfuls of phlegm,
six handfuls of bile,
and the entire remainder were drawn out by the wind.
It was filled with one āḍhaka of blood and six prasthas of feces, each of these being equal and distinct from one another.
It is enveloped by seven layers of skin and possesses six tastes;
it is constantly entered by bile and the bodily fire (kāyāgni), which is born from the Agnihotra sacrifice and is mobile.
With its foul extremities, it is difficult to behold with all its bodily parts;
its very nature is a stench.
What self-conceit or state of great esteem can there be for this?
It should be understood by one whose mind is fixed on the Dharma as being like a borrowed vessel for a momentary purpose, or like a cart for the carrying of a load.
Beholding such a body as this— a heap of impurities—
the one who conceives pride in form dwells in a state of delusion; for he is a person of childish intellect, perceiving what is known [as the body] to be the world itself.
The vehicle goes, but not the driver.
"Carrying a long-lasting form that appears pleasant, yet always carrying [within it] what must be discarded;
the body of a living being is utterly impure, like a worm—how then can there be passion or great esteem for it?
Reflecting in this manner, and so forth.

It is just as if, monks, there were a granary open on both sides, filled with various kinds of grain—sesame, mustard, mung beans, barley, and black lentils—and a man with good eyesight, looking into it, would know: "These are awned grains;
these are podded grains."
In the same way, monks, a monk contemplates this very body—just as it is situated, just as it is disposed—up to [the point of] detailed observation.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced and frequently cultivated, leads to the abandonment of sensual desire.
In that regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life?

In this regard, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, thoroughly drenches, fills, and suffuses this very body internally and individually with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
He makes it thoroughly pervaded;
there is no part of his entire body that remains unpervaded or unsuffused by the joy and happiness born of seclusion within himself.
Monks, it is just as if blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, or white lotuses were born in the water.

Submerged in water, they are all drenched, soaked, filled, saturated, and suffused with cool water. In the very same way, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, [contemplates] this very body internally.
He drenches, permeates, fills, suffuses, and gladdens himself with the joy and happiness born of seclusion within his own person.
There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded—that is to say, by the joy and happiness born of seclusion internally.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to happiness in the present life.
It conduces to dwelling in peace.
In this regard, monks, what is the cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision?
Here, monks, a monk has properly and thoroughly grasped the perception of light;
he has attended to it well, seen it clearly, and firmly established it, and he cultivates a mind that is equally luminous, sustained by the perception of day.
As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day;
as before, so after.
As it is behind, so it is in front;
as it is below, so it is above;
as it is above, so it is below—with a mind thus expanded, he dwelt [in equanimity].
With a mind bound by the perception of day, he cultivates a state of even radiance.
Monks, it is just as if, in the last month of summer, on a cloudless day when the sky is free of clouds, at the time of midday, the light becomes utterly pure, completely cleansed, and luminous;
it is not [otherwise] than that.

It happens thus at the time of darkness. In the same way, monks, when a monk has properly and thoroughly grasped the perception of light— unconfused, well-established, and free from the perception of novelty—
he cultivates a mind of even radiance, such that as it is by day, so it is by night, and as it is by night, so it is by day.
As it was before, so it is after;
as it is after, so it was before;
as it is above, so it is below; as it is below, so it is above—with an expanded mind, unobstructed, established in the perception of day, he cultivates a mind of equal radiance.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge, vision, and eloquence.
In this regard, what is the cultivation of concentration that, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of wisdom?
Here, a monk, having gone to the forest...

Or, having gone to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling, through the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
This cultivation of concentration, when practiced, developed, and cultivated repeatedly, leads to the attainment of wisdom.
These are the four cultivations of meditative concentration.
[13] In this regard, monks, what are the four foundations of mindfulness?

Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the external body...

He dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in internal feelings, in external feelings, and in both internal and external feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating the mind in the internal mind, in the external mind, and in both internal and external minds, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, in external phenomena, and in both internal and external phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world;
these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
[14] In this regard, monks, what are the four right efforts?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.
He exerts vigor,
restrains the mind,
and correctly applies it.
He generates desire, exerts himself, and arouses vigor for the abandoning of unwholesome states that have arisen.
He exerts the mind and applies it thoroughly;
he generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
He exerts himself, arouses vigor,
and uplifts the mind.
He applies himself correctly;
for the stability, cultivation, non-confusion, non-decline, further increase, growth, expansion, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen, he generates desire,
exerts himself, and strives.
One exerts vigor,
upholds the mind, and correctly applies oneself;
these are the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).

[15] In this regard, what are the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)? Here, monks, a monk cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment; it is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. This... his energy will be neither slack nor over-exerted. (2)

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and the formative forces of abandonment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my mind not become overly slack, nor overly exerted. (3)

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration through investigation, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment, [thinking]: "May my investigation not be too slack, nor too strained. // 4 //
Monks, these are the four bases of psychic power.
[16] In that regard, monks, what are the five faculties?
Namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
In that regard, what is the faculty of faith?
By means of which faith one has faith in four things?
Which four? One maintains the mundane right view that pertains to the realm of saṃsāra.
He takes refuge in the ripening of karma,
thinking: "Whatever action I shall perform, whether wholesome or unwholesome, I shall experience the ripening of that very action."
Even for the sake of his life, he does not perform an evil deed;
this is called the faculty of faith.
In that regard, what is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*)?
It is those phenomena which one has faith in by means of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
One brings it to fulfillment by means of the faculty of vigor;
this is called the faculty of vigor.
In that regard, what is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
Those phenomena which one brings to fulfillment through the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), those very phenomena one [consolidates] through the faculty of mindfulness...
...it causes [the mind] not to be lost.
This is called the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya).
In that regard, what is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?
Those phenomena which one makes one-pointed by means of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*),
those very phenomena one penetrates by means of the faculty of wisdom.
He becomes one whose nature is to investigate those phenomena;
this is called the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties.
[17] In that regard, monks, what are the five powers?
Namely: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
And these are called "powers" because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions, which act like servants.
Monks, these are the five powers.
[18] In that regard, monks, what are the seven factors of enlightenment?

Namely: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
In this regard, monks, a monk cultivates the factor of awakening that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
In this way, he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of awakening that is energy, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is joy, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment.
[19] In this regard, monks, what is the noble eightfold path?
It is as follows: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, monks, is called the noble eightfold path.
In that regard, what is right view?

It is that which is supramundane, not arisen from the view of a self, nor from [the views of] a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, a human, or a man; not arisen from the views of annihilationism or eternalism; not arisen from the views of existence or non-existence; and not arisen from views that are wholesome or indeterminate.
And that which does not arise from the views of saṃsāra or nirvāṇa is called right view.
In that regard, what is right intention? It is not to form those intentions by which the afflictions of passion, hatred, and delusion arise.
He forms those volitions by which the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of liberation arise;
this is called right intention.
In that regard, what is right speech?
It is that by which one does not torment oneself or others through passion,
nor does one afflict oneself or others.
He does not harm himself or others;
he is endowed with that speech which is composed and disciplined,
by which he correctly instructs and advises.
This is called right speech.
In that regard, what is right action?
It is that one does not perform any action which is black and has a black ripening.
That karma which is black-and-white and has a black-and-white ripening— that karma he does not perform;
that karma which has a black-and-white ripening and is entirely black...
It conduces to the destruction of karma; he performs that karma.
One performs wholesome actions;
one whose sphere of activity has wholesome actions as its refuge— this is called right action (samyakkarmānta).
In that regard, what is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*)?
It is the state of relinquishing for the sake of one's purpose through the refinement of virtues, being free from hypocrisy, flattery, extortion, hinting with words,
and longing for future worlds.
Contentment with one's own person and one's world, freedom from deficiency, and a livelihood known by the noble ones—
this is called right livelihood.
In that regard, what is right effort? It is that effort which is false, which is underlain by the latent tendencies of the afflictions— ignorance, attachment, aversion, and delusion.
He does not desire that exertion;
rather, he pursues that exertion which correctly leads one into the truth of the Noble Path and provides the practice that goes toward Nirvana.
This is called right effort.
In this regard, what is right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*)?

It is that mindfulness which is well-established, unshakable, straight, and not crooked; which perceives the faults and dangers of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and leads one along the path to nirvāṇa; it is the pervasive awareness and the non-forgetfulness of the noble path.
This is called right mindfulness.
In that regard, what is right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)?
It is the concentration that is characterized by correctness.
Abiding in which concentration, for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings, one enters into the state of being correctly established and the path of certainty (*niyāma*).
This is called right concentration;
this is called the noble eightfold path.
[20] In this regard, monks, what is mindfulness of breathing in its sixteen aspects?
Breathing in short or long, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in."
Breathing out long, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in short.
Or, breathing out short, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out short."

Experiencing the body while breathing in, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the body. Experiencing the body while breathing out, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing the body.
Experiencing the bodily formations while breathing in, one understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the bodily formations."
Experiencing the bodily formations while breathing in, or experiencing the bodily formations while breathing out, one understands it as it truly is.
Experiencing the whole body while breathing in, one understands as it truly is: "I am breathing in experiencing the whole body.
Experiencing the bodily formations while breathing in, or not experiencing the bodily formations while breathing out, one understands it as it truly is.

He understands: breathing in while experiencing the whole body, he understands as it really is, "I am breathing in while experiencing the whole body"; breathing out while experiencing the whole body, he understands as it really is, "I am breathing out while experiencing the whole body. Breathing in while experiencing all bodily formations, and breathing out while experiencing all bodily formations... [he understands as it really is, "I am breathing out while experiencing all bodily formations"].

He understands as it really is: "I am breathing out while experiencing [the breath]. He understands as it really is: "Calming my bodily formations, I am breathing in; calming my bodily formations, I am breathing in. He understands as it really is: "Calming my bodily formations, I am breathing out; calming my bodily formations, I am breathing out."

Experiencing rapture while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing rapture. Experiencing rapture while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing rapture."

Experiencing pleasure while breathing in, he knows as it truly is: "I am breathing in experiencing pleasure. Experiencing pleasure while breathing out, he understands as it truly is: "I am breathing out experiencing pleasure. Experiencing the mind while breathing in, he understands as it truly is: "I am breathing in experiencing the mind."

Experiencing the mind while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out experiencing the mind. Experiencing the mental formations while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in experiencing the mental formations. (AvSū)
He understands as it really is:
"Experiencing mental formations, I am breathing out; experiencing mental formations, I am breathing out. [While] breathing in, he understands as it really is:
"My mental formations are becoming tranquil."
He understands as it truly is:

"I am breathing in while calming the mental formations"; he understands as it truly is: "I am breathing out while calming the mental formations"; he understands as it truly is: "My mind is gladdening as I breathe in"; he understands as it truly is: "My mind is gladdening as I breathe in."

"My mind gladdens as I breathe out; my mind gladdens as I breathe out"—thus he understands it as it really is. "My mind is liberated as I breathe in; my mind is liberated as I breathe in"—thus he understands it as it really is.
"My mind is liberated as I breathe out..."
His mind becomes settled; he understands as it really is: "I am breathing out with my mind settled.
Breathing in with his mind settled, he understands as it really is: "I am breathing in with my mind settled."
With a concentrated mind, while breathing out, he understands as it really is: "My mind is concentrated as I breathe out.

Likewise, contemplating impermanence, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment, while breathing in, he understands as it really is: "Contemplating relinquishment, I am breathing in. ... Or, while breathing out, contemplating relinquishment, he understands as it really is: "Contemplating relinquishment, I am breathing out."
Monks, this is mindfulness of breathing in sixteen aspects.

[21] In that regard, what are the four factors of stream-entry? Here, monks, a disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, thinking: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One: a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."

"The Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One"—thus, through verified clarity regarding the Dharma, he becomes endowed with faith: "The Dharma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise, namely, the state of the taming of pride and the destruction of thirst."

It is the complete subduing [of defilements], the uprooting of the substrate (*ālaya*), the cutting off of the phenomena, the non-apprehension of emptiness, the exhaustion of craving, cessation, and nirvāṇa.

He becomes endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha: "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s noble disciples has practiced well; it has practiced rightly, practiced appropriately, practiced correctly, and practices in accordance with the Dharma, living according to the Dharma."
In the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry;
in the Saṅgha there are stream-enterers;
in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning.
In the Saṅgha there are those who are once-returners;
in the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning;
in the Saṅgha there are those who are non-returners.
In the Saṅgha there are those practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship;
in the Saṅgha there are arhats— namely,
the four pairs of persons.
There are eight types of persons.

This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, endowed with faith, endowed with learning, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, and worthy of reverential salutation with joined palms.

He is worthy of proper homage, an unsurpassed field of merit, and beautiful to behold for the world— namely, one who is endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, stainless, liberating, ungrasped, well-composed, praised by the wise, leading to victory, and irreproachable by the wise.
These are the four factors of stream-entry.
[22] Monks, what are the ten powers of a Tathāgata?
The Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the possible as possible, and he understands, as it truly is, the impossible as impossible.
This is the first power of the Tathāgata:
he understands, as it truly is, the ripening of the undertaking of karmic actions belonging to the past, future, and present.
He understands, as it truly is, the ripening of the various inclinations of other beings and other persons.

He understands, as it truly is, that the world of many world-systems is a world of diverse elements. He understands, as it truly is, the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings.
He understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere that leads to various destinations.

He understands, as it truly is, the defilement and purification of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments of other beings. With their aspects, their members, and their specific characteristics, he recollects his manifold previous existences.
He recollects even a single birth;

he recollects two, three, four, and so on, up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of births—such is the detailed account. With the divine eye, which transcends that of humans, he sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn.
"By means of the good and bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, [beings] are reborn in happy and miserable destinies," and so forth in detail.
"Through the destruction of the outflows, he understands with wisdom, as it truly is, the untainted liberation of the mind.
These, monks, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
[23] Monks, what are the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) of the Tathāgata?
Herein, the Blessed One knows himself to be perfectly awakened (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

Regarding this, no one in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, could raise a challenge, saying: "These dharmas have not been fully awakened to by you."
The Tathāgata, the Blessed One, perceives this sign; perceiving the sign, he realizes the state of the bull, having attained security and fearlessness;
having entered the assembly, he roars the lion’s roar.

He sets in motion the Brahma-wheel, which has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding those things declared by the Tathāgatas to be obstructive conditions, for one who indulges in them, no one can legitimately bring a charge that they do not constitute an obstruction; such is the detailed explanation.
Or rather, as for this noble path declared by him to be leading to liberation— if, while disregarding the inferior [path],
one were not to go forth by means of the other for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering— regarding this point, someone [objects] as before.

When one who has exhausted the outflows (kṣīṇāsrava) declares himself to be such, if anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, and among the race of gods and humans, were to bring forth a challenge, saying, "These outflows have not been fully exhausted," the Tathāgata perceives no such ground for such a claim.
Perceiving no such ground, the Tathāgata dwells having attained stability, having attained fearlessness, and is joyful.
He understands his own standing;
having entered the assembly rightly, he roars the lion’s roar and turns the Brahma-wheel, which has not been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, or anyone else in the world in accordance with the Dharma.
Monks, these are the four grounds of self-confidence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata.
[24] What are the Tathāgata’s four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?

Namely: the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
These, monks, are the four analytical knowledges.
[25] Monks, what are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
The Tathāgata has no physical lapse, and he has no vocal outcry.
There is no loss of mindfulness, there is no unconcentrated mind,
and there is no perception of diversity.
There is no equanimity lacking discernment;
there is no loss of zeal; there is no loss of vigor.
There is no loss of mindfulness, no loss of wisdom,
and no loss of liberation.
The three knowledges and visions of liberation:
the knowledge and vision that is unattached and unimpeded regarding the past time; [and likewise regarding the future and the present].
Unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future time;
unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present time;
and the transformation of perception preceded by knowledge in all bodily actions.
All verbal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.
Monks, these are the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
[26] In that regard, what are the thirty-two marks of a great person of the Tathāgata?
Having well-placed feet is a mark of a great person of the Tathāgata;
having the soles of the feet marked with wheels on the undersides of both soles is [another].
The heels are broad and well-proportioned;
the fingers and toes are long; and the hands and feet have webbed membranes.
The quality of having soft and youthful hands and feet; the quality of having a body with seven prominent parts; and the quality of having shanks like those of the eneya antelope.
The state of having the private parts enclosed in a sheath;
the state of having the upper body like that of a lion; and the state of having well-filled shoulders.
The well-restrained shoulders;
the lack of protuberance [on the chest]; and the long-reaching arms.
Purity of the eyes;
a neck like a conch shell;
and a jaw like that of a lion.
He has forty even teeth;
his teeth are even and without gaps;
his teeth are brilliantly white.
A long and slender tongue;
a sense of taste that perceives the finest flavors;
and a voice like that of Brahmā or the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
The quality of having deep blue eyes;
the quality of having eyelashes like those of a cow; the quality of having delicate skin.
The skin is golden-colored;
each pore has a single hair;
and the body hairs are upright and curl to the right.
The hair is as dark as sapphire;
there is a tuft of white hair (ūrṇā) between the eyebrows on the forehead;
and the head is crowned by a protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
The symmetry of a banyan tree and universal loveliness; the strength of Mahānārāyaṇa and universal loveliness—
this is a mark of a great person belonging to the Tathāgata, the Great Person.
Monks, these are the marks of a great person belonging to the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s feet are well-placed; this mark of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) was produced in the past through his firmness in undertaking commitments. On the soles of his feet there are wheels marked upon the soles; this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past through his not acting deceptively toward other beings. His heels are long and his feet are well-proportioned; this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was brought about in the past through his honoring his parents and serving at their feet.
The long fingers: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past by providing protection, shelter, and guardianship for the Dharma.
The webbed hands and feet: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past by not causing division within retinues.
The soft and tender hands and feet: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was produced in the past by the gift of various garments and food.

The body having seven protuberances—this mark of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata was produced by his being ever-ready and well-disposed toward the tasks of others. ... The purity of the eyes—this mark of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata was produced by his former diligent undertaking of the ten paths of wholesome action.

The conch-like neck—this mark of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata was produced in the past by his giving various medicines and food to the sick. The lion-like jaw—this mark of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata was produced in the past by his application of roots of virtue. The possession of forty even teeth—this mark of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata was produced in the past by his application of comforting sentient beings.

The quality of having teeth without gaps—this mark of a great person (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata arose in the past through his bringing together those beings who were divided. The quality of having even teeth—this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata arose in the past through his giving of pleasing jewels. The quality of having very white teeth—this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata arose in the past through his well-guarded actions of body, speech, and mind.
The long and slender tongue— this mark of a great person (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata was brought about in the past by his speaking the truth.
The supreme sense of taste— of the Tathāgata...
The mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) of a person arises from having previously accumulated an immeasurable mass of merit and from being supremely devoted to self-restraint.
The quality of possessing a voice like that of Brahmā or the *kalaviṅka* bird— this mark of a Great Man of the Tathāgata arose from having previously spoken kindly words to sentient beings.

The quality of having eyes that are deep blue arises from hearing pleasant words. This mark of a great person (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata arose in the past through protecting sentient beings with loving-kindness (*maitra*).
The quality of having eyelashes like those of a cow arises from this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata; it arose in the past through [protecting]... (apra-).
It was produced through the accumulation of merit.

The quality of having delicate skin—this mark of a great person (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata—was produced by his previous karma of protecting the mind during the communal recitation of the Dharma. The quality of having golden-colored skin—this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata—was produced [by the same cause].

The quality of having body hairs that grow individually was produced in the past by providing agreeable bedding, seats, and coverings, and by giving pleasant speech. The quality of having body hairs that curl to the right— this mark of a Great Man belonging to the Tathāgata— was produced in the past by avoiding social crowds and by respectfully receiving the instructions of teachers, preceptors, and spiritual friends.

The quality of having hair as dark blue as sapphire: this mark of a great person (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata was brought about in the past by his compassion for all living beings and by his refraining from using clods of earth, sticks, or weapons.

The quality of having a white ūrṇā-hair between the eyebrows on a forehead that is well-defined: this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was brought about in the past by his speaking in praise of those worthy of praise.
The quality of having a protuberance on the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa): this mark of a great person of the Tathāgata was brought about in the past by his bowing with reverence toward his teachers.

The body being well-proportioned like a banyan tree and being pleasing from every side—this mark of a great man of the Tathāgata was produced in the past by his application of himself and other beings to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The body being pleasing from every side—this mark of a great man of the Tathāgata [was produced] in the past... [by his application of himself and other beings to meditative concentration].
It was produced by means of fashioning images of the Tathāgata, by restoring ruined stūpas, and by providing consolation and support to others who were afraid.
Furthermore, because he possessed mastery over those qualities through immeasurable roots of virtue, the thirty-two marks of a great person were produced upon the body of the Tathāgata.
[27] What are the eighty minor marks?
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have copper-colored nails;
they have glossy nails; they have prominent nails; they have rounded fingernails; they have well-proportioned fingers; and they have tapering fingers.

His veins are hidden and free from knots, his ankles are concealed, and he walks with the stride of a lion, the stride of an elephant, the stride of a swan, and the stride of a bull; he moves clockwise, he moves gracefully, his limbs are straight, his limbs are rounded, his limbs are well-proportioned, his body is broad and heavy, and his secondary marks are perfectly complete.

They have even strides, pure limbs, soft limbs, and purified limbs; their limbs are well-developed, well-knit, and with well-proportioned minor members; their eyes are clear and free from darkness; their bellies are rounded, smooth, and unmarred; they have slender waists, deep navels, and spiraling navels; they are pleasing to behold on all sides and are pure in their conduct.

Their bodies are free from moles; their hands are as soft and delicate as cotton; the lines on their palms are glossy, deep, and clearly defined; their faces are not overly long; their teeth are like the reflection of a bimba fruit, perfectly aligned and without gaps; their tongues are soft and copper-colored; their voices have the resonance of an elephant’s trumpeting or a thundercloud, being sweet, profound, and charming; and their fangs are rounded, sharp, even, and tapered.

They have prominent noses, pure noses, and wide eyes; their eyebrows are long, their eyes are like blooming lotuses, and their eyes are like the petals of the blue lotus; their eyes are broad and full, their brows are long, their brows are even in hair, and their brows are glossy; their ears are full and long, their ears are symmetrical, and their ears are unimpaired.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess well-rounded foreheads, perfectly full [facial features], hair resembling bees, circular hair, white hair, untangled hair, non-rough hair, and beautiful hair; and the soles of their feet bear the marks of the śrīvatsa, svastika, nandyāvarta, wheel, vajra, lotus, fish, and so forth.
Monks, these eighty secondary marks have been manifested upon the body of the Tathāgata.

As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; I proclaim the holy life (brahmacarya) which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and purified—namely, the discourse on the Dharma called 'The Determination of Meaning' (Arthaviniścaya). This is what was stated therein.
"Monks, dwell in forest retreats, empty huts, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces under the sky, cemeteries, and forest thickets... Monks, do not be negligent;
do not become remorseful later.
This is my instruction."
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those monks and that entire assembly—the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.
The noble Dharma discourse titled "The Determination of Meaning" is completed.
